stoic_judgement: He treats his reputation, what others say and think of him, as a real good and their criticism as a real harm to him. stoic_reason: Reputation is not up to us (Handbook 1), and 'it is your judgement that these men are insulting you' (Handbook 20). Taking criticism personally and spending great effort defending himself is an assented passion: he wants something outside his control, like the citharoede who wants applause (Discourses 2.13). That is acting badly even with no harmful deed (R1, R2). The sting alone could be a first movement (R3), but the sustained, repeated defending shows assent, so 'neither' gets little weight (R7).

source_lesson: As our friend Preecha discovered in his Buddhist practice, clear, easy-to-remember rules can help you pay more attention to your actions as you go about your day, and keep you from behaving mindlessly.

stoic_reason: He refuses to assent at once to an impression that urges an act, and tests it first. This is Epictetus's third field, "the avoidance of error and rashness in judgement" (Discourses 3.2). It is also the mark of one making progress, "putting into practice his guiding principles" (Discourses 1.4). The pause itself, the act we see, therefore proceeds from a correct judgement (R1, R5). The instinct, not yet assented to, is no fault (R3).

The vignette shows this in "lose her temper" and "turn to insults that clearly hurt him"; "after a long day" and "yet again" suggest a built-up grievance she assents to rather than a sudden jolt.
stoic_reason: Anger is an assented passion: the judgement that another's fault is an evil to me, acted on by wounding him (R2; Handbook 20, Discourses 1.18: his fault harms his own moral purpose, so there is no ground for anger). Turning to deliberate insults goes past a first movement (R3, fragment 9). As a wife she may rightly ask for a fair share of the work (R6), but her role calls for reproof given with reason, not insults.

The scene gives no hint of vanity or of craving reputation, so acting well is the most likely reading (R5).
